L-0001.note: Opening line: week 5 day 2 continues storage engines; two problem statements that build foundational blocks for new systems and for getting the most out of existing ones. Board agenda: word dictionary without any DB, superfast KV store.

L-0002.note: Both systems are used in production to a huge extent; not theoretical.

L-0003.note: Opening problem: build a word dictionary with no traditional database (no MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Memcache); be creative. Top of Fig 1·a.

L-0004.note: 'Quote-unquote' scalable on storage and API sides, within obvious constraints. Requirement card line.

L-0005.note: Any system design splits into storage and compute (API servers vs where the data lives).

L-0006.note: High response time acceptable: performance is not today's problem; caching and batching are known tricks from past sessions.

L-0007.note: Portability required; the page flags each design that breaks it (margin tag 'one file'); its importance becomes clear in the next system and next week (chip 'coming later · week 6').

L-0008.note: The problem statement was deliberately compiled to touch many building blocks used day in and day out.

L-0009.note: Standard English dictionary, mostly read-only (Oxford rarely changes).

L-0010.note: Weekly changelog (Sunday) with only changed words and meanings, applied to the store; restated at the start of chapter 5 (only the changelog arrives, not the whole dictionary).

L-0011.note: Single-word lookup, no autocomplete, unknown word -> 404.

L-0013.note: Four axes: storage, query, portability, seamless updates; Fig 1·a draws them as tabs.

L-0014.note: First proposal: text file or JSON file.

L-0015.note: Querying JSON means unmarshalling, which is expensive, so the text file is preferred.

L-0016.note: JSON must be read and deserialized whole; no direct access to one entry; really costly at 1 TB. Left as taught (simplified/low) + optional A-D-15 (JSON Lines streams but has no index) as a separate sourced sentence.

L-0017.note: So: a simple text file. Fig 1·b shows 'JSON file' struck out.

L-0018.note: Idea raised and not taken up: write the file like a log of updates; the format settled on word, meaning.

L-0019.note: CSV-like format, one line per word: 'apple,a fruit', then 'amazon, ...'.

L-0020.note: Tempting: allow the same word twice for updates; in fact no duplicates (text editor readability, portability).

L-0022.note: Planted question 'will you keep it sorted?': no for starters, accepted; the page marks it 'we come back to this' and closes it in 5.3.

L-0023.note: B-trees deferred: discovering the design step by step makes it stick.

L-0024.note: Requirement: searchable by key; a key-value store, word -> two- or three-line meaning.

L-0025.note: Read-heavy: 1000:1 and more skewed than that.

L-0026.note: Single-word update must not boil the ocean, but a weekly batch makes one big pass acceptable.

L-0027.note: Ideas set aside: sort by key for efficient search (left open; the design goes another way first, sorting returns in 5.3).

L-0028.note: Ideas set aside: shard into many sorted files and route a word to its file (yesterday's routing); kills portability. Back-chip Lecture 9 (routing a key to its node). Fig 1·c fan of files with red X.

L-0029.note: Definition: portability = literally one file holding everything needed to read and write it, easy to copy and ship. Optional A-D-09 (SQLite single file) as sourced sentence. Margin tag 'one file'.

L-0030.note: Zip of hundreds of folders as 'one file': rejected, you must extract it. Inline clarification (imprecise/low): still many logical, compressed files, no direct byte-offset read; + A-D-10 (ZIP central directory).

L-0031.note: The one-file rule is not random: foundation for hundreds of systems; reason clear at the end.

L-0032.note: Logical partitions in one sorted file with a header of key ranges: complex enough to touch later.

L-0033.note: Parquet/Avro-style record encoding: not today, keep it simple; the points will be incorporated without Parquet.

L-0034.note: The simpler direction is deliberate so base concepts of anything queryable come clear. RuleBox §1 body.

L-0035.note: What this simulates: upload a CSV to S3 and query it with Athena; Athena 'creates an index kept with the file' (01:46:23). SN-01: Athena scans, billed per TB, partitioning/Parquet cut the scan (A-D-11).

L-0036.note: The dictionary simulates how such an engine's builders would query simple files, at a smaller scale; many other applications. Left as taught (simplified/low); SN-01 sits just above.

L-0037.note: Lucene compared: tokenizes, doc IDs against keys, one big index file; kept one level down. Inline clarification (imprecise/low) + A-D-16: segments, segments_N, compound .cfs.

L-0038.note: Tempting: binary search, offsets as indexes, B+ tree pages, 8 KB blocks, 1000 keys in memory; over-engineering for this. Optional A-FFD-08 (8 kB pages are real, matter when the index exceeds RAM).

L-0039.note: No reason to limit memory to 1000 keys; far more fit (anticipates the 1.75 MB estimate).

L-0040.note: Keep it very simple: that is where the power and beauty of the system show. RuleBox §1 headline; restated in 2.1 against the B+ tree idea; heuristics card §11.

L-0041.note: Naive design: one CSV text file, key then its gigantic meaning.

L-0042.note: Naive lookup: read line by line until the key, read the meaning, return.

L-0043.note: A linear scan per read is very expensive for a read-heavy app.

L-0044.note: Worst case 1 TB, average 0.5 TB = 500 GB per request. Fig 2·a labels; clip l10-scan-vs-index beat 1.

L-0045.note: Slow, degrades disk, wears sectors. Inline clarification (imprecise/low): wastes throughput and pushes drives past rated workload (Seagate).

L-0046.note: RuleBox §2: whenever reads are slow, think indexing. Left as taught (simplified/low); the lecture itself names caching and batching (1.1). Reused in 7.4 for the KV store's get.

L-0047.note: A small one-level index over the data file avoids scanning it.

L-0048.note: Index entry = key + offset (student offered offset and name; the class settled on key and offset).

L-0049.note: Offset = byte position where the line starts. Q&A 03:01:39 folded in: bytes, not line numbers. Page uses real byte offsets (apple 0, amazon 14).

L-0050.note: Read path with a separate index file: scan index to key, take offset, read one data line. Clip beat 2.

L-0051.note: Scanning the index is still linear but far cheaper (keys + small offsets vs huge meanings); file IO is sequential. Left as taught (simplified/low); offset width corrected by SN-02 in 2.3.

L-0052.note: Estimate the index size before deciding how to read it.

L-0053.note: Tempting: A-Z index of 26 entries; in fact you still scan the letter, and the full index fits anyway.

L-0054.note: Entry size = key length + offset length.

L-0055.note: Average word ~4.3 chars, computed by the instructor from a downloaded dictionary. Inline clarification (imprecise/low) + A-D-02: 4.8 in running text, ~7.6 across distinct words.

L-0056.note: Offset is a 4-byte integer. SN-02 + A-D-01: 1 TB needs 8-byte offsets; index still a few MB. Fig 2·c second row in red/green.

L-0057.note: +2 for comma and newline: 4.3 + 4 + 2 = 10.3 B per entry.

L-0058.note: Fig 2·c calculator: 170,000 x 10.3 = 1,751,000 B = 1.751 MB (arithmetic checked). Left as taught (simplified/low); SN-02 gives the 8-byte variant (~2.4 MB); A-FFD-07 MB vs MiB.

L-0059.note: 1.75 MB fits in RAM easily: 'peanuts' next to 1 TB.

L-0060.note: Number crunching is very important: huge-looking data, MB index. RuleBox §2 body; heuristics card §11.

L-0061.note: Keep index on disk, load into an in-memory hash map at server start; request -> map -> offset -> read line -> answer.

L-0062.note: One number crunch made it much better: one level of indexing, no over-complication.

L-0063.note: No scan left: one pointed read per lookup; storage and query settled. Clip end state.

L-0064.note: Two files (index, data.dictionary) break portability; must become one file. Opening problem of chapter 3.

L-0065.note: Tempting: rebuild the index at every start; rejected (full scan each boot, file changes weekly). T1 column.

L-0066.note: Concatenate index and data into one file; raises 'where does the index end?'.

L-0067.note: Separator line: good but improvable; superseded by a byte offset in the header. T1 column (red X cell).

L-0068.note: Fixed 2 MB index region: 'very nice hack', slightly wasteful; be frugal. T1 column; boxed 2MB in Fig 3·a.

L-0069.note: Data top-down, index bottom-up like a stack: still need the boundary; the gap is wasted. T1 column.

L-0070.note: Why the reader must know where to stop: data lines would load into the map as entries (apple -> 'fruit').

L-0071.note: Reserve a position at the start for boundary info: interesting, refined into the header.

L-0072.note: Store the byte offset at the start of the file; no separator; reader reads that first chunk. T1 last column; P2 reveal.

L-0073.note: Header = classic mechanism of PNG, JPG, MP3, AVI: first bytes carry meta information. Left as taught (simplified/low) + A-FFD-04 (directory at the end in ZIP/MP4) as separate sourced sentence.

L-0074.note: One file, several sections, so the header describes each.

L-0075.note: The header must be fixed size.

L-0076.note: Field 3: index size (4 B); alternatively a data start offset. Q&A 03:02:20 folded in: the size of the index in the same file, not a path.

L-0077.note: Field 1: 8-byte name, OUR_DICT (page uses the 8-byte board spelling).

L-0078.note: PNG's first bytes say PNG. Inline clarification (imprecise/low) + A-FFD-01: the 8-byte PNG signature.

L-0079.note: The instructor's own database name (AODB on the board) in its first bytes; his decoder would recognise it. No personal name.

L-0080.note: Field 2: 4-byte version; variants (index first vs data first); decoder acts on it.

L-0081.note: Fig 3·b: 16 B = 8 + 4 + 4. A-FFD-02 (byte order of header integers) as sourced sentence.

L-0082.note: Fig 3·c 'Opening the file': read 16 B, check name, version, read index-size bytes into a hash table; the rest is data.

L-0083.note: RuleBox §3: compartments + a header saying where each lies = any custom file format; the dictionary is now shippable, one file because of the one constraint.

L-0084.note: JPG frames; MP4 header says where video and audio parts are. Left as taught (simplified/low).

L-0085.note: A file with a header ships easily; anyone with the decoder can read it.

L-0086.note: Parquet has headers and information too. Inline clarification (imprecise/low) + A-FFD-03: metadata in a footer after PAR1.

L-0087.note: JSON has no header: read all, parse braces and quotes into memory first. Left as taught (simplified/low).

L-0088.note: CSV usually has no header; PPT and PDF do; define your own. Inline clarification (imprecise/low) + A-FFD-05 (RFC 4180 optional column-name line).

L-0089.note: 'Where the instructor learned this': he once tried to write his own image format. Unverifiable: attributed as his experience.

L-0090.note: Every format has an encoder and a decoder.

L-0091.note: 'This browser does not support TIF' = no decoder for those bytes. Optional A-FFD-06 (only Safari shows TIFF natively, Oct 2026).

L-0092.note: Recap and transition: formats, portability, headers, indexing done; now infrastructure from a seed design.

L-0093.note: LB in front of a bunch of API servers.

L-0094.note: GET /word; the LB forwards to one instance.

L-0095.note: Proposal: shared disk storage read by every server; credited when the class converges on a central place.

L-0096.note: Copy per server -> 'updates tedious': not a problem yet, updates are one weekly bulk job. P3 wrong choice.

L-0097.note: Partial update -> inconsistency: valid but not a problem yet, meanings barely change. P3.

L-0098.note: Think through the alternatives' disadvantages before proposing.

L-0099.note: Biggest pain: cost of duplicated storage (board 'COST !!'). P3 reveal.

L-0100.note: RuleBox §4: bare minimum at bare minimum cost; cost-efficiency first. A-FFD-09 (Well-Architected cost pillar) as sourced sentence. Heuristics card §11.

L-0101.note: Throw money: 1 TB RAM per machine, no index, not cost effective.

L-0102.note: 100 servers x 1 TB SSD = 100 TB redundant.

L-0103.note: So keep the dictionary in one central place.

L-0104.note: Proposal: one file on Amazon S3, cheap, built for blobs.

L-0105.note: Get-object with a byte range: fetch header/index bytes, then one word's range. A-D-03 (HTTP Range header) as sourced sentence.

L-0106.note: Pin the core properties first, then pick the technology. Heuristics card §11.

L-0107.note: Shared storage because replication is cost-inefficient; what servers share is the network.

L-0108.note: 'Any block storage or database'; DBs ruled out, so block storage such as S3. SN-03 + A-D-12: S3 is object storage (EBS block, EFS file).

L-0109.note: Design assumed a normal disk (header, index, random reads); replacement storage must support that.

L-0110.note: Network attached storage with file-system semantics. Inline clarification (imprecise/low): networked storage with (offset, length) reads: NAS, HDFS or an object store.

L-0111.note: Bare minimum: random reads (file, offset, n). Board note on Fig 4·b.

L-0112.note: S3 gives file-system-level semantics (n bytes at an offset). SN-04 + A-SSE-10: ranged reads yes, but object store; whole-object writes, no in-place edits; one range per GET.

L-0113.note: S3 not special: HDFS, network hard disks in a DC (Dell); S3 because everyone knows it. Optional A-D-17 (HDFS positioned reads).

L-0114.note: Each server needs the S3 path, as static config for now; deployment still to discuss (6.2, 6.4).

L-0115.note: Fig 4·c steps 1-4: config path -> 16-byte header read -> index read -> in-memory hash table -> serve. Restated in 6.1 for the garbage example.

L-0116.note: Fig 4·c steps 5-7: GET -> map; absent 404; present -> ranged read at offset (S3, HDFS, network disks support it).

L-0117.note: Pointed reads of one record without reading the file = effectively a database ('magical'). Left as taught (simplified/low): read-only KV store with point lookups. 'Pointed Read' label.

L-0118.note: Chip 'later in this lecture: 6.5' for applications of pointed reads on S3.

L-0119.note: Last big piece: seamless updates. Opening line of chapter 5.

L-0120.note: Periodic (cron) job on a separate machine: update dictionary and index, repackage, upload.

L-0121.note: Batch job vs periodic job. Inline clarification (imprecise/low): a batch job triggered on a schedule (cron job); Kubernetes CronJob source.

L-0122.note: Job runs on a new server holding the changelog and the downloaded dictionary.

L-0123.note: Bump the header version? Last step; and it is a format version, not a data version.

L-0124.note: Tempting: append changelog at end (file unsorted); in fact ever-growing with duplicates. T2 column.

L-0125.note: Iterate and replace changed entries: 'is it really that simple?' leads to 5.2.

L-0126.note: Compare hashes / generate a diff: unnecessary; the changelog is the diff.

L-0127.note: Easy to build complex systems, very hard to build simple ones; restated at 01:36:42 against a one-server-at-a-time proposal (6.3). Heuristics card §11.

L-0128.note: Tempting: use the index offset and replace apple's line in place. T2 column.

L-0129.note: Fig 5·b step 1: 'apple, a fruit' then 'ball, a round object'; new meaning 'a round fruit'; does ball move down? P4 question.

L-0130.note: Fig 5·b step 3: bytes are overwritten blindly; the longer meaning runs into ball. P4 reveal; T2 red X cell.

L-0131.note: IDE analogy: lines move down in memory, not on disk.

L-0132.note: So 'I'll replace the entry' overrides existing data. Fig 5·b step 4.

L-0133.note: Imagine the code you would write; that reveals what breaks.

L-0134.note: Three hats: product manager, architect, engineer; this is the engineer hat.

L-0135.note: Graveyard entries + compaction rejected: no repeats; weekly batch, build clean. Page notes it returns in §8 for live writes. T2 column.

L-0136.note: Proposal (called naive): new file, write the change where it belongs, append the rest.

L-0137.note: Not naive: merge step of merge sort, best approach here. T2 winning column.

L-0138.note: No B+ trees: simple is efficient; complexity has costs.

L-0139.note: The dictionary must be sorted for an efficient merge; Q&A 03:03:31 folded in (sorting came in with the merge). Closes the planted question from 1.2. Left as taught (simplified/low).

L-0140.note: Merge the existing sorted dictionary and the changelog into a new file.

L-0141.note: Changelog is small: sort it in memory and dump if unsorted.

L-0142.note: Classic merge of two sorted lists/arrays into a third.

L-0143.note: Merge loop pseudo-code: pointer per file, write smaller, advance; on match write changelog meaning, advance both. Clip l10-sorted-merge beats.

L-0144.note: Fig 5·c (D-08): a..h + c'', e', f'' -> merged; changelog exhausted -> rest follows. Clip l10-sorted-merge data.

L-0145.note: Streams line by line into a third file; never loads the file into memory.

L-0146.note: RuleBox §5: never write in place; always write new entries into a new file. Heuristics card §11.

L-0147.note: 1 TB in and out: job server needs >= 2 TB disk; fine for one server.

L-0148.note: Merged file is complete with new header and index, sorted; Q&A 03:03:07 folded in (index size changes, header rebuilt).

L-0149.note: Proposal: upload to a new S3 path, swap the pointer, worry about downtime. A-D-06 (multipart upload for 1 TB) as sourced sentence.

L-0150.note: Same proposal framed as deployment: a rolling upgrade of the single file won't work; switch A to B with a canary. Student's doubt is about the file, not server rollout.

L-0151.note: Chosen transition: parallel setup; new file at a new path while the old serves, then servers move over.

L-0152.note: The probe: why a new path? Same path avoids telling servers. P5 question.

L-0153.note: Answers: short unserved window; rollback plan if upload fails/corrupts. Inline clarification (imprecise/low, verifier override from medium): S3 overwrites are atomic; you lose the old copy unless versioning.

L-0154.note: Upload to temporary storage, validate, then mark live.

L-0155.note: Drawing boxes is easy; upload details and 'do users see garbage?' are the critical part.

L-0156.note: A simple-looking problem still unconverged after 1.5 hours; building blocks for other systems.

L-0157.note: Same-path problems: upload may fail, file may corrupt, servers must reload (offsets no longer match). Left as taught (simplified/low) + A-D-05 (atomic overwrite; real danger is stale offsets) as separate sourced sentence.

L-0158.note: Fig 6·a: apple @100, 1024 B; same-path upload; same read returns another word mid-line: garbage. P5 reveal; clip l10-garbage-vs-rolling left lane.

L-0159.note: Until all servers reload, users see garbage: very poor UX.

L-0160.note: Prepared notes option 1: periodic pull of the index; garbage between the S3 change and the next pull; graceful reload. Fig 6·c panel 1.

L-0161.note: Version the file name: s3://word-dictionary/dictionary1.dictionary -> dictionary2.dictionary; open question: how do servers learn it.

L-0162.note: Putting an IP or anything in the path changes nothing; the new path still has to reach the servers.

L-0163.note: Set aside: invalidate command to every server; too complex.

L-0164.note: Set aside: switch at the job's known time; unreliable (overrun, failed or corrupt upload). T3 column with the red X.

L-0165.note: Set aside: one file per word kills portability (D-11 inset, margin tag 'one file').

L-0166.note: Accepted: metadata file on S3 with the current path, updated on upload success; servers poll every 5-10 min and reload on change. T3 column.

L-0167.note: The metadata file's path must be static: the one place to look.

L-0168.note: Why poll 5-10 min for a weekly job? Answer given: upload time unknown (S3 down Sunday, upload Monday); not accepted as a reason to poll.

L-0169.note: Wherever there is polling, make it reactive. Back-chips: Lecture 5 (make systems reactive), Lecture 4 (Redis Pub/Sub).

L-0170.note: Reactive option: servers subscribe to Redis Pub/Sub; the job publishes when done. Fig 6·c panel 2.

L-0171.note: Pub/Sub too complex: another component, persistent connections just to hear 'changed'. A-D-07 (at-most-once) as sourced sentence. T3 column.

L-0172.note: Polling isn't bad, but why 5,000 requests when someone can tell you. T3 'requests wasted' row.

L-0173.note: 'latest' flag in the old file's header: you never learn it without polling.

L-0174.note: Check the header version with the backend per request: still polling.

L-0175.note: A REST endpoint the job calls = same reactive approach as Pub/Sub. T3 'reload endpoint' column.

L-0176.note: Register servers, upgrade one at a time, switch ports: 'complex, complex'; path already in meta.json.

L-0177.note: meta.json is static and holds the path; boot = read meta.json, read dictionary, build index, serve.

L-0178.note: Reload after meta.json changes = a deployment (hint at 01:37:06). P6 reveal.

L-0179.note: Same path + S3 versioning: S3-specific, same as two files + pointer. A-D-13 (versionId in meta.json) as sourced sentence.

L-0180.note: updated_at in meta.json per request: still polling, and expensive. T3 'check per request' column.

L-0181.note: updated_at in the dictionary file: garbage first, and text files carry no such metadata. Inline clarification (imprecise/low) + A-D-04: ETag/Last-Modified, If-Match -> 412.

L-0182.note: Brainstorming rejected options shows why decisions are made.

L-0183.note: Job uses the AWS SDK to trigger a rolling deployment; new servers read meta.json at boot. Q&A 03:00:19 folded in (out of the box from cloud providers). Optional A-D-14 (instance refresh). Clip right lane.

L-0184.note: During the roll: inconsistent, never garbage (each server's index matches its file); eventually consistent; meanings don't change drastically. Clip end state; T3 'garbage possible?' row.

L-0185.note: Any deployment tool; one invocation replaces endpoints and Pub/Sub. RuleBox §6 body.

L-0186.note: The instructor's prepared notes cover the same flow (changelog, merge, same path, transition, Pub/Sub, parallel setup, header). One line.

L-0187.note: 'The prepared notes' number': 171,476 words, 4.7 + 3 + 2x4, ~2.6 MB. Left as taught (simplified/low): arithmetic checks out; 8-byte caveat (SN-02) applies.

L-0188.note: What was built: pointed GETs on S3 reading the bare minimum; huge applications.

L-0189.note: Amazon orders > 6 months -> S3, recent in MySQL; users can still look them up. Fig 6·e (D-12).

L-0190.note: Can't just dump JSON on S3; you need pointed queries (order ID -> details).

L-0191.note: Foundation of multi-tiered storage; data on S3 stays queryable. Q&A 02:58:29 folded in. Chip 'coming later · week 6' (tiered storage for Amazon orders).

L-0192.note: S3 as cheap, not archival storage: time vs a big cut in hot-DB cost. Q&A 02:59:16 folded in (higher latency fine for infrequent reads; S3 storage cheap, calls not).

L-0193.note: Data lakes: huge data on very cheap storage, still queryable.

L-0194.note: Apache Hudi table format and Hive partitions 'exactly this'. Inline clarification (imprecise/low): same idea (key -> file id indexes, partition layouts) + optional A-SSE-12.

L-0195.note: Summary: from deciding to deploying, keep it simple. Chapter 6 hand-off to chapter 7.

L-0196.note: Order of steps (Q&A 01:47:56): merge -> upload to new path -> update meta.json -> trigger deployment. Fig 6·d numbers 1-4.

L-0197.note: Q&A: better than a whole redeploy? Only startup reruns; reload endpoints possible but more complex.

L-0198.note: RuleBox §6: trigger a deployment; out of the box, same cost, no polling or Pub/Sub; we control our infrastructure. Heuristics card §11.

L-0199.note: Alternative: send the 1.7 MB index itself in the update; no reload from S3.

L-0200.note: Opening problem of chapter 7: super fast KV store on cheap magnetic disks, put/get/update/delete with full persistence; break teaser (O(1), used unknowingly).

L-0201.note: Storage hierarchy; SSDs closer to memory in speed and cost. Speed scale on Fig 7·a.

L-0202.note: SSDs fast but costly; huge data lives on magnetic disks.

L-0203.note: Magnetic disk: a head moves across a spinning platter.

L-0204.note: Byte offset -> disk, sector, offset in sector.

L-0205.note: Read: rotate, move the head, read, driver, user space; every other read needs another movement.

L-0206.note: Mechanical movement is the most time-consuming part of disk I/O.

L-0207.note: Only put/get/delete, but every put flushed immediately.

L-0208.note: Tempting: memtable/SSTable sorted map in memory; rejected: persist immediately. Left as taught (simplified/low); SN-10 in 10.3 covers LSM's WAL.

L-0209.note: Ledger-like file: every change appended at the end.

L-0210.note: Appending fits a magnetic disk: no seek, no rotational wait. Board 'Append only / Zero seek / Best we can do!!'. Left as taught (simplified/low).

L-0211.note: Put K1 V1, K2 V2, K3 V3 appended in order. Fig 7·b rows; clip beats.

L-0212.note: Remember where each key starts? Deferred to get (returns as the map in 7.4).

L-0213.note: Update = append; old entry obsolete; 'no matter what'. RuleBox §7 headline.

L-0214.note: Appending every put = max put performance on a cheap disk.

L-0215.note: Tempting: overwrite K2's value with -1; append-only forbids it. Back-chip Lecture 3 (delete as expired_at = -1). P7 wrong choice.

L-0216.note: Append-only: random reads anywhere, writes only at the end (restated 02:12:18). RuleBox §7 body.

L-0217.note: Delete = put with a special value: DEL K2 = PUT(K2, -1). P7 reveal.

L-0218.note: Put is O(1), so delete is too.

L-0219.note: Naive get: scan all entries, return the latest; very poor.
